segments.text: Investigative techniques are methods used to obtain, test and organize information.

Interviewing usually seeks an account from a person; interrogation is more accusatory or suspect-focused in common usage and must remain within law and rights safeguards. Analysis connects facts, timelines, links and behavioural patterns.

Information may come from complainants, witnesses, records, surveillance authorized by law, forensic examination, public sources and cooperating agencies. Investigators should distinguish raw information from verified evidence and record the source, time and circumstances in which it was obtained.
Triangulation improves reliability: a claim becomes stronger when independent records, physical evidence or other testimony support it.

An investigative interview seeks an accurate account and should use open questions, careful listening, clarification and appropriate challenge. Leading or coercive practices can contaminate memory and increase the risk of unreliable statements. The objective is information quality, not simply a confession.

Interrogation of a suspect is governed by legal and ethical safeguards. Voluntariness, access to counsel where required, protection from torture or coercion and accurate recording are essential to reliability and admissibility.

Criminal investigative analysis may compare offence behaviour, locations, timing, victim selection and modus operandi to generate hypotheses about possible links or offender characteristics. Such analysis is an investigative aid, not proof of identity.
Its conclusions should be expressed probabilistically and tested against independent evidence. Overconfident profiling can narrow an investigation too early and produce tunnel vision.

items.text: Information gathering includes witnesses, records, surveillance where lawful, databases, digital sources and physical evidence. Each source has reliability and legal limits.

An interview is generally information-seeking and should encourage a complete account. An interrogation is more suspect-focused or accusatory in common usage and therefore carries greater risk of coercion or false confession if poorly conducted.
Open questions encourage narrative detail; focused questions clarify facts; leading or coercive questioning can contaminate memory or reduce reliability.
Criminal investigative analysis organizes timelines, links, locations, communications, finances and behaviour to identify patterns and test competing explanations.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not present aggressive pressure as a sign of effective interrogation. Lawful, ethical and evidence-based questioning is more defensible and often more reliable.

items.text: Study open/closed questioning, corroboration and documentation.
Avoid endorsing coercive or unlawful practices.

segments.text: Confession is not a substitute for corroborated evidence.
Ethical interviewing improves legitimacy and reliability.
